## Overview

A model in `CellularAutomataCore.jl` says nothing about where its state lives or
how its cells are visited; that is the **backend**, chosen when the problem is
solved:

| backend | state | best for |
|---|---|---|
| `ReferenceBackend()` | plain arrays, boundaries applied on every access | checking the others |
| `ArrayBackend(; threaded)` | padded arrays, optionally threaded | most models |
| `SparseBackend(background; tilesize)` | only tiles that differ from the background | invasions across large, mostly empty landscapes |
| `GPUBackend(device)` | arrays on a GPU (or any KernelAbstractions device) | very large lattices |

Every backend gives **exactly** the same result for the same problem, stochastic
rules included, because random numbers are a function of the seed, the cell,
the time and the draw number rather than of the order of computation. The test
suite checks every backend against `ReferenceBackend` on a battery of problems.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
using KernelAbstractions
```

## One model, every backend

A stochastic SIR epidemic, solved on each backend:

```{julia}
sir = LocalRule(VonNeumann(1)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    if cell == 0
        return bernoulli(ctx, 1 - (1 - ctx.p.β)^count(==(1), nbrs), 1) ? Int8(1) : Int8(0)
    elseif cell == 1
        return bernoulli(ctx, ctx.p.γ, 2) ? Int8(2) : Int8(1)
    end
    return cell
end
n = 256
u0 = zeros(Int8, n, n)
u0[n ÷ 2, n ÷ 2] = 1
prob = CAProblem(sir, u0, 300, (β=0.6, γ=0.2); seed=1)

backends = ["Reference" => ReferenceBackend(),
            "Array, serial" => ArrayBackend(threaded=false),
            "Array, threaded" => ArrayBackend(threaded=true),
            "Sparse" => SparseBackend(Int8(0); tilesize=32),
            "GPU (KernelAbstractions CPU)" => GPUBackend(KernelAbstractions.CPU())]
results = map(backends) do (name, backend)
    solve(prob; backend, save_everystep=false)              # compile
    t = @elapsed sol = solve(prob; backend, save_everystep=false)
    (name=name, seconds=round(t; digits=3), final=final_state(sol))
end
[(r.name, r.seconds) for r in results]
```

```{julia}
all(r.final == results[1].final for r in results), Threads.nthreads()
```

All five agree exactly. The second number is the thread count this document was
rendered with.

The KernelAbstractions CPU device runs the GPU code path on the CPU, which is how
it is tested without a GPU. On a machine with a GPU, load its package and pass
its device, or let `GPUBackend` take the device from an array:

```julia
using CUDA                      # or AMDGPU, Metal, oneAPI
backend = GPUBackend(CUDABackend())
backend = GPUBackend(CuArray(zeros(1)))   # the same, from an array
```

GPU rules must be usable inside a kernel: states and parameters that are plain
bits types (numbers, `Bool`s, isbits structs, `NamedTuple`s of them), and
functions that do not allocate. `Symbol` states and graph spaces run on the CPU
backends only.

## Apple GPUs with Metal

On a Mac, `using Metal` makes the Apple GPU available as `MetalBackend()`. Metal
has no double precision, so a GPU-ready rule uses `Float32` parameters and
literals: `bernoulli` then draws in single precision, and `Stochastic(0.5f0)`,
`KernelField(...; precision=Float32)` and `Lenia(; precision=Float32)` keep
everything in `Float32`. The code below runs only where Metal is available.

```{julia}
has_metal = Sys.isapple() && Base.find_package("Metal") !== nothing
if has_metal
    @eval using Metal
    has_metal = Metal.functional()
end
has_metal
```

```{julia}
if has_metal
    metal = GPUBackend(MetalBackend())
    sir32 = LocalRule(VonNeumann(1)) do c, n, ctx
        c == Int8(0) && return bernoulli(ctx, 1.0f0 - (1.0f0 - ctx.p.β)^count(==(Int8(1)), n), 1) ?
                              Int8(1) : Int8(0)
        c == Int8(1) && return bernoulli(ctx, ctx.p.γ, 2) ? Int8(2) : Int8(1)
        return c
    end
    p32 = CAProblem(sir32, u0, 300, (β=0.6f0, γ=0.2f0); seed=1)
    same = final_state(solve(p32; backend=metal, save_everystep=false)) ==
           final_state(solve(p32; backend=ArrayBackend(), save_everystep=false))
    println("Float32 SIR on Metal identical to the CPU: ", same)
    lenia = CAProblem(Lenia(; precision=Float32), rand(Xoshiro(3), Float32, 512, 512), 30)
    for (name, backend) in ["CPU, threaded" => ArrayBackend(threaded=true), "Metal" => metal]
        integ = init(lenia; backend, save_everystep=false)
        step!(integ, 2)
        t = @elapsed step!(integ, 10)
        println(rpad(name, 14), round(1000t / 10; digits=1), " ms per Lenia step (512², R = 13)")
    end
else
    println("Metal is not available here; on an Apple-silicon Mac, add Metal to the environment.")
end
```

The epidemic is identical on the GPU, because its random numbers do not depend
on the order of computation. Lenia's 27 × 27 kernel makes each step
compute-heavy, which is where a GPU pays off; Float32 Lenia on the GPU agrees
with the CPU to rounding, since GPU implementations of `exp` differ in the last
bits.

## Which backend supports what

```{julia}
schemes = [Synchronous(), Stochastic(0.5), Checkerboard(), RandomSequential(), Margolus()]
names_ = ["Reference", "Array", "Sparse", "GPU"]
bs = [ReferenceBackend(), ArrayBackend(), SparseBackend(0), GPUBackend(KernelAbstractions.CPU())]
[(name, [string(nameof(typeof(s))) for s in schemes if supports(b, s)]) for (name, b) in zip(names_, bs)]
```

## Sparse storage for invasions

`SparseBackend` cuts the lattice into tiles and stores and updates only tiles
that hold a cell differing from the background state. Early in an invasion
that is a tiny fraction of the landscape, so the cost per step follows the
infested area rather than the lattice size. The rule must leave a background
cell with all-background neighbours unchanged; the backend checks a sample of
cells when the problem is set up.

```{julia}
n = 2048
v = zeros(Int8, n, n)
v[n ÷ 2, n ÷ 2] = 1
large = CAProblem(sir, v, 120, (β=0.6, γ=0.2); seed=2)
for (name, backend) in ["Array, threaded" => ArrayBackend(threaded=true),
                        "Sparse" => SparseBackend(Int8(0); tilesize=32)]
    integ = init(large; backend, save_everystep=false)
    step!(integ)  # compile
    t = @elapsed step!(integ, 119)
    extra = backend isa SparseBackend ? ", $(stored_tiles(integ)) of $(cld(n, 32)^2) tiles stored" : ""
    println(rpad(name, 18), round(1000t / 119; digits=2), " ms per step", extra)
end
```

After 120 steps the epidemic covers a small part of the 2048 × 2048 lattice:
the sparse backend stores a few dozen of the 4096 tiles and is many times
faster per step than updating every cell (the timings are from the machine
that rendered this document). As the epidemic spreads, the advantage shrinks;
once most tiles are active, the dense backend is faster.

## Choosing a backend

- Start with the default `ArrayBackend()`: threaded when Julia has more than
  one thread, any scheme, any space.
- For invasions or outbreaks on large landscapes that are mostly in one state,
  try `SparseBackend(background)`.
- For very large lattices with isbits states and synchronous, stochastic or
  checkerboard updating, use `GPUBackend`.
- When results look wrong, compare with `ReferenceBackend()`: it is the
  definition the others are tested against.
